intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Hoxha-Aliu syndrome (HXAL) is caused by homozygous null mutation in the ERI1 gene on chromosome 8p23.1.

checks.explanation: Paper reports a single patient with a homozygous nonsense variant in an autosomal recessive syndrome; generalization to 'null mutation' causing the named syndrome goes slightly beyond this single case.

checks.explanation: ERI1 lies in the deleted 8p23.1 region.

paragraphs.text: Hoxha-Aliu syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are developmental delay or mild intellectual disability and abnormalities of the distal limbs, including brachydactyly, clinodactyly, brachytelephalangy, short metacarpals, nail dysplasia, and syndactyly (Hoxha and Aliu, 2023; Guo et al., 2023). Some patients also had cardiac malformations (Choucair et al., 2017). The disorder results from biallelic null variants in ERI1. Biallelic ERI1 missense variants cause a different and more severe phenotype, spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (Guo et al., 2023).

checks.evidence_quote: ERI1: A case report of an autosomal recessive syndrome associated with developmental delay and distal limb abnormalities.
checks.explanation: Title describes the syndrome as autosomal recessive.

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) studied patients with congenital NAD deficiency disorder. One of them (F5.II.1) was a girl homozygous for a missense variant in KYNU who also carried a homozygous loss-of-function variant in ERI1 (see MOLECULAR GENETICS). Her cardiac findings were a perimembranous ventricular septal defect and pulmonary vein stenosis. She had reduction defects of the hands and feet. The right hand showed a transverse terminal limb reduction with a rudimentary fifth digit. The left hand had hypoplastic, deep-set nails on several digits. On the right foot, digits 1 and 5 had no nails and digits 2 to 4 were absent. On the left foot, digits 3 to 5 were absent, digits 1 and 2 had no nails, and there was syndactyly. Other features were microcephaly, global developmental delay, and autism. Craniofacial features included brachycephaly, a flat occiput, bitemporal narrowing, a small nose, and cupped, prominent ears. She also had bilateral inguinal hernias. Szot et al. (2021) noted that her limb and cardiac abnormalities resembled those of the patient reported by Choucair et al. (2017).

paragraphs.text: Szot et al. (2021) used trio exome or genome sequencing in a girl (F5.II.1) with limb reduction defects, cardiac anomalies, microcephaly, developmental delay, and autism. She was homozygous for a missense variant in KYNU, glu206-to-lys (E206K). She was also homozygous for a loss-of-function variant in ERI1, c.514C-T (gln172-to-ter; Q172X). In yeast complementation assays, the KYNU variant was among those with the mildest effect on NAD levels. Szot et al. (2021) suggested that the ERI1 variant might partly explain her distinct phenotype and could confound the role of mild NAD deficiency. They noted that the functional link between ERI1 mutation and these defects had not been assessed.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2023) identified biallelic ERI1 variants in 8 affected individuals from 7 unrelated families. Individuals with biallelic null variants had mild intellectual disability and digital anomalies. The 5 individuals with missense variants had severe spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia. The missense variants caused loss of exoribonuclease activity, which led to defective trimming of the 3-prime end of 5.8S rRNA and decreased degradation of replication-dependent histone mRNAs. Induced pluripotent stem cells derived from affected individuals showed impaired chondrogenesis in vitro, with downregulation of genes that regulate skeletal patterning.
